title: Workflows and agents: who owns the control flow

items.stem: Your team is describing the difference between a workflow and an agent in a design review. Which statement separates the two correctly?

options.text: An agent can call tools, while a workflow cannot call any tool
An agent runs on a larger model, while a workflow runs on a smaller one
In an agent the model picks the next step; in a workflow the code does
An agent takes many steps, while a workflow takes only one step

items.stem: A makerspace assistant's code works like this. Step 1: ask the model to label the student's message as 'question' or 'booking'. Step 2: if the label is 'booking', the code looks up the calendar; otherwise the code searches the manuals. Step 3: ask the model to write the reply. The steps and the branch are written in the code. How should you classify this design?

options.text: A workflow, because the code decides the order of the steps and the branch
An agent, because the model makes a decision when it labels the message
An agent, because the model is called more than once for each request
A workflow, because it does not use a language model at any of its steps

items.stem: Which part of the makerspace assistant is the best candidate for a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

options.text: Working out why a student's 3D print keeps failing, using several manuals
Answering vague questions that might need any of several different tools
Helping a student plan which machines a new project will need
Booking a slot when the student has given the machine, date and time

items.stem: For a task whose steps are always the same, in one sentence, why is a fixed workflow usually a better choice than an agent? Think of your sponsor's budget and of what you can promise at the design review.

The assistant's code always checks the student's training record first, then always looks up the booking calendar, then hands the results to a model that may call tools in a loop until it writes the reply. Who owns the control flow?

options.text: The code owns all of it, so the whole design is a workflow
The code owns the first two steps; the model owns the loop in the last step
The model owns all of it, since a model writes the final reply
Neither owns it, because a mixed design has no owner of its flow

items.stem: Every model call costs $0.02, whatever its length. A fixed booking workflow makes exactly 2 model calls per request. An agent handling the same booking requests makes 6 model calls per request on average. For 500 booking requests, how many dollars more does the agent cost than the workflow?
